mechanisms.precedent: a: Stripe's idempotency keys (Stripe API docs, 'Idempotent requests': the first result is stored under the key and given to retries); AWS Lambda Powertools' idempotency utility (a record is claimed INPROGRESS with an in-progress expiry before the handler runs, then set COMPLETED with the stored result; a changed payload is an error; confirmed by search); Temporal and Restate for a re-run that issues the same ids and is stopped when it diverges. | b: Stripe's idempotency keys (API docs, 'Idempotent requests'); AWS Lambda Powertools idempotency (a conditional claim with an in-progress expiry, then the stored result); for a re-run that must issue the same effects, Temporal's replay against its event history (a command that differs is a non-determinism error)
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state (per key: a claim with a lease, then the first result, for a ttl), same rules, same role. Not modelled beside `sess` (E-20 modelled `keys` alone). For V4 it applies only if v4 were built on. | b: Same state (per key: a claim with a lease and the first result), same rules (claim before the handler runs; a retry gets the first result; a re-run repeats the same effect ids), same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Cursor mark beside the outputs (srchi-slot)
mechanisms.state: Per consumer, source slot and output slot: the highest source sequence applied, written in the output's own entry. Where a row has no slots the key is the output's own moving unit; that carry was not modelled.
mechanisms.rules: Apply an output only above the mark and write the source sequence into its entry; commit the consumer's cursor only after every output of the record is answered; carry the slot's marks out with the fence and in with the open.
mechanisms.model: E-30: 5 rules by ablation (6 of 6 mutants); real Elle agrees on 2,800 histories
mechanisms.source: AMENDMENTS A-05 (all rows; replaces SPACE 4.2's retention-length table); precedent on offer: storing consumer offsets beside the outputs (KafkaConsumer javadoc); for V4 it would apply only if v4 were built on
mechanisms.precedent: a: KafkaConsumer javadoc, 'Storing Offsets Outside Kafka' (keep the consumed offset in the same store, and the same atomic write, as the results; after a restart skip what is at or below it); Helland, 'Life beyond Distributed Transactions' (CIDR 2007), 'activities': the receiving entity keeps, inside itself, what it has taken from each partner, and that state moves with the entity; Delta Lake's SetTransaction(appId, version) action in its log protocol. | b: Apache Pulsar: PIP-6 keeps, in the output topic's own log, the last sequence id per producer, and Pulsar Functions' effectively-once mode uses one producer per input and the source message id as that sequence id; Delta Lake's transaction identifiers (PROTOCOL.md: appId and version written inside the commit; options txnAppId and txnVersion); KafkaConsumer javadoc, 'Storing Offsets Outside Kafka'
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Three of E-30's five rules are that pattern as it stands: write the mark in the output's own entry, apply only above it, commit the cursor after. One mark per output slot is what the pattern means when the output store has many units and no transaction across them (Helland's entities). The other two rules carry the marks on a slot move; they belong to the move's carried set (A-17) and are counted in slot-move. A close call: AMENDMENTS leaves it open. For V4 it applies only if v4 were built on. | b: Same state (per source and per output unit, the highest source position applied, written with the output itself), same rules (apply only above the mark; commit the reader's cursor after the outputs), same role (derived outputs once, with no time horizon in Delta and in the Kafka pattern). The key per output slot is the analogue of 'per output partition': the mark lives in the unit that moves. The carry on a move is a rule of the slot move, which is counted novel there. A-05 leaves this open; close call. checked on the web on 2026-11-10 (Pulsar and Delta).

mechanisms.name: Writer time (the median of the members' clocks)
mechanisms.state: Per group: the last time stamp t in its log; and each member's view of its peers' clocks, carried forward by its own monotonic clock.
mechanisms.rules: The writer stamps each batch with max(last t, the median of the members' clocks); t never goes back, across a handover too. TTL expiry and lease lapse are judged by t on the writer's tick and written as log entries (A-23).
mechanisms.model: E-21: 7 rules by ablation, on a seeded simulation (30 seeds in each of nine families), not exhaustive
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 T `clamp`; DESIGN-V5 4.2 'The writer's time'; AMENDMENTS A-23 and D1; precedent on offer: CometBFT's BFT time
mechanisms.precedent: a: CometBFT's BFT Time (spec/consensus/bft-time.md: a block's time is the weighted median of the validators' clock readings, and it never goes back; confirmed by search). TigerBeetle's cluster time (src/vsr/clock.zig and 'Three Clocks are Better than One', 2021: each replica samples its peers' clocks on pings, carries the readings by its own monotonic clock, takes the interval most clocks agree on, and the primary's timestamps only rise; confirmed by search). For expiry written into the log by the leader's time: Ongaro's thesis, section 6.3, and Redis, whose master expires a key and replicates the DEL. | b: CometBFT's BFT Time (spec/consensus/bft-time.md: a block's time is the median of the validators' vote times, and it never goes back); Ongaro's thesis section 6.3 for expiry by a time carried in the log; etcd's lease revoke as a log entry
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state (the last time in the log; each member's view of its peers' clocks), same rules (stamp max(last, a middle value of the members' clocks); judge TTLs and leases by it at the writer), same role. The draft's clamp is TigerBeetle's form; A-23's median is CometBFT's, which E-21 cites. | b: Same state (the log's last time; the members' clock readings), same rules (stamp the median; never back; expiry judged by the log's time and written as entries), same role (a log time that one wrong clock cannot move). The readings come from pings here and from votes there. SPACE called it '1 small'. checked on the web on 2026-11-10 (BFT Time).

mechanisms.name: Timestamp oracle
mechanisms.state: In the controller: the last timestamp handed out, and a high-water window saved before it is used.
mechanisms.rules: Every transaction takes its start and commit timestamps from the oracle's leader; timestamps strictly rise, across a controller failover too. It is also the time by which TTLs and leases are judged.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 T `tso`; TiKV PD, Percolator; not modelled here
mechanisms.precedent: a: Percolator's timestamp oracle (Peng and Dabek, OSDI 2010, section 2.3); TiKV PD's TSO. | b: Percolator's timestamp oracle (Peng and Dabek, OSDI 2010); TiKV PD's TSO, which saves a window before it hands timestamps out
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: It is PD's own mechanism. PD only. | b: The published mechanism. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Lock rows (#locks)
mechanisms.option: saga (the saga's locks; P-10's locks in every row that can judge a condition)
mechanisms.state: Per lock: its holder, its lease end and its version; the version is the fence token.
mechanisms.rules: A lock is claimed only when its row is absent or its lease has lapsed by writer time; the claim's new version is the token. A saga's locks belong to the unit (A-24); a lock name has one lease (A-10).
mechanisms.model: E-24: inside the saga's 38 rules by ablation; E-21 (simulated) for leases under clock faults
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 X `saga`; DESIGN-V5 5.3 'Locks'; AMENDMENTS A-24, A-10; REQUIREMENTS P-10
mechanisms.precedent: a: Chubby (Burrows, OSDI 2006, section 2.4: locks and sequencers); etcd's clientv3/concurrency Mutex (a key made only if absent and bound to a lease; its create revision is the fence token). | b: Chubby (Burrows, OSDI 2006: locks with sequencers); etcd's lock on a lease, with the key's revision as the token; Kleppmann, 'How to do distributed locking', 2016
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state (per lock: holder, lease, a version that is the token), same rules, same role. E-24 counts these rules as published. | b: Same state (holder, lease end, a version that is the token), same rules (claim when absent or lapsed), same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Fence tokens (the fence table)
mechanisms.state: Per group, carried with a moving slot: the highest token seen per lock.
mechanisms.rules: A protected write carries its lock's token; the writer refuses a token below the highest it has seen for that lock, and raises the table on a write it takes. A slot move carries the table, merged by max. Writers do not follow #locks (A-24).
mechanisms.model: E-24: inside the saga's 38 rules; E-17: 1 fence-transfer rule in every move; E-21 (simulated): the fence refused every late write under every time rule
mechanisms.source: DESIGN-V5 5.3 'Locks' and 10.2 (fences); SPACE 2 O (fence tokens are positions) and K `hyb`; AMENDMENTS A-24, A-17 (carried); E-44 (on BUY fencing is by convention)
mechanisms.precedent: a: Chubby, section 2.4 (a server checks a sequencer 'against the most recent sequencer that the server has observed'); Kleppmann, 'How to do distributed locking' (2016): the store keeps the highest token it has seen and refuses a lower one. | b: Chubby section 2.4 (a server may check a sequencer against the most recent one it has seen); Kleppmann 2016 (the store keeps the highest token and refuses a lower one); HDFS QJM epoch numbers at the journal nodes
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state (the highest token seen per lock, at each place that takes protected writes), same rule, same role. With 'writers follow #locks' dropped (A-24), what is left is exactly the published form. The carry on a slot move is counted in slot-move. | b: Same state (the highest token seen per lock, at the place of the write), same rules, same role. The carry on a move is a rule of the slot move. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Saga intent rows (#sagas)
mechanisms.state: Per unit: its steps and its direction (run, undo, then done or undone).
mechanisms.rules: Take the unit's locks in key order, write the intent, apply each step under its fence, record done. A holder first resolves another unit's unfinished intent on its partitions; a failed run undoes every step, the failed one and those after it too (A-24).
mechanisms.model: E-24: 38 rules by ablation with 'undo every step' (41 of 44 mutants; 1 novel rule as E-24 counts it); E-22, E-22b (simulated, real Elle)
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 X `saga`; DESIGN-V5 5.3; AMENDMENTS A-24 and D5 (BUY takes it in fero's L5 library)
mechanisms.precedent: a: Garcia-Molina and Salem, 'Sagas' (SIGMOD 1987): the saga's log and backward recovery. Percolator (Peng and Dabek, OSDI 2010, section 2.2): whoever meets an unfinished transaction resolves it first. For 'undo every step, the ones that never ran too': Seata's TCC mode (seata.apache.org, 'Seata TCC fence', v1.5.1, table tcc_fence_log: Cancel runs for a branch whose Try never arrived, the 'empty rollback', and leaves a record so that a late Try is refused, the 'suspension' case; confirmed by search). Kafka's epoch bump (KIP-98) is the precedent for A-24's other form. | b: Garcia-Molina and Salem, 'Sagas', SIGMOD 1987 (the saga log, backward recovery); Percolator (resolve another transaction's lock first); for 'a failed run undoes every step': the TCC pattern's empty rollback and anti-hanging rules as Apache Seata builds them (tcc_fence_log since 1.5.1: a cancel for a branch whose try never ran writes a marker, and a late try is then refused); Kafka KIP-98's end markers and epoch bump
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: E-24 found 37 of its 38 rules published and one new: a failed run undoes every step, and the undo is the write that shuts a late step out. That is the same rule in the same role as Seata's empty rollback with its fence record, which E-24 did not know. So I count 0 novel rules, and I do not need Kafka's end markers for it. Same state (an intent row per unit, with its direction), same rules, same role. | b: Same state (an intent with its direction), same rules, same role. E-24 counted 1 novel rule, 'undo every step', where the undo also raises each partition's fence. That is TCC's cancel of a branch that never ran, which also blocks the late try: same rule, same role, in production. So 0 novel rules. Close call. checked on the web on 2026-11-10 (Seata).

mechanisms.name: Two-phase commit (transaction records and intents)
mechanisms.state: Per transaction: a primary lock and secondary locks (intents) on the keys it writes, and its commit record at the primary.
mechanisms.rules: Prewrite every key with a lock that names the primary; commit the primary at a commit timestamp, then the secondaries; a reader that meets a lock resolves it from the primary. A retried commit finds its record: the transaction id is the dedup key.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 X `2pc`, D `txn`; Percolator, TiKV; not modelled here
mechanisms.precedent: a: Percolator (Peng and Dabek, OSDI 2010, section 2.2); TiKV's transaction model. | b: Percolator (OSDI 2010); TiKV's transactions
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: It is TiKV's own mechanism. PD only. | b: The published mechanism, as PD's row takes it. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Multi-version rows (MVCC)
mechanisms.state: Per key: its versions by commit timestamp, and a safe point below which old versions are collected.
mechanisms.rules: A committed write adds a version at its commit timestamp; a read at timestamp t sees the newest version at or below t; versions below the safe point are collected.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 5 (X `2pc` forces O `hlc` or T `tso` and a multi-version S); SPACE 4.2 PD; TiKV; not modelled here
mechanisms.precedent: a: Percolator's data, lock and write columns (OSDI 2010, section 2.2); TiKV's MVCC with its GC safe point. | b: TiKV's MVCC with a GC safe point; Percolator
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: It is TiKV's own mechanism. PD only. | b: The published mechanism. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Transaction coordinator log
mechanisms.state: Per transactional id, in the coordinator's own log: its producer id and epoch, the transaction's state and the partitions it wrote.
mechanisms.rules: The coordinator records begin, then prepare-commit or prepare-abort, writes a marker to every partition and records the end. A new producer with the same id bumps the epoch and fences the old one.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 X `ktxn`; Kafka transactions (KIP-98); not modelled here
mechanisms.precedent: a: Kafka transactions (KIP-98: the transaction coordinator and its __transaction_state log). | b: Kafka's transaction coordinator (KIP-98)
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: It is Kafka's own mechanism. ISR only. | b: The published mechanism. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Commit markers and the last stable offset
mechanisms.state: Per partition: commit and abort markers in its log, and the last stable offset, below which no transaction is open.
mechanisms.rules: The coordinator writes a marker for each partition of an ended transaction; a read_committed reader stops at the last stable offset and skips aborted records.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 X `ktxn`; Kafka transactions (KIP-98); not modelled here
mechanisms.precedent: a: Kafka transactions (KIP-98: control records and the last stable offset). | b: Kafka's control markers and last stable offset (KIP-98)
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: It is Kafka's own mechanism. ISR only. | b: The published mechanism. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Memory rung (a replica that stops uncleanly rejoins as new)
mechanisms.state: Per replica: whether it stopped cleanly. Under `memory` an acknowledged tail may not be on its disk.
mechanisms.rules: A commit under `memory` waits for a majority to hold the entry in memory, with disks within about a second. Each replica marks whether it stopped cleanly. A replica that stopped uncleanly cannot vouch for its log; disk-incarnation's rule then brings it back as a new replica that never votes under its old identity.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 Q `maj-m`, `mix`; DESIGN-V5 4.1 and decision 4b; Kafka's default, Redpanda write caching; AMENDMENTS section 2 Q (its safety was never modelled: G-05, K-09); E-02 (speed measured)
mechanisms.precedent: Kafka with acks=all and no fsync (its default): a record commits once the in-sync replicas hold it in memory; each log dir has a clean-shutdown marker; a broker that stopped uncleanly leaves the eligible leaders (KIP-966) and counts toward commits again only after it has caught up and rejoined the in-sync set. Viewstamped Replication Revisited (Liskov and Cowling, MIT-CSAIL-TR-2012-021, sections 4 and 4.3): commit at a majority in memory, and a replica that crashed takes no part until it has recovered its state from the others. The step 'come back as a new replica' is disk-incarnation's rule (Paxos Made Live, section 5.1; KIP-853), counted there.
mechanisms.why: Referee. DESIGN-V5 4.1 writes one rule with three triggers: 'a replica that cannot vouch for its log comes back as a new replica' (a new disk, damaged records, an unclean stop under memory). So a's regrouping is taken: that rule sits in disk-incarnation, and the memory rung keeps two things, a clean-stop mark and the commit rule. Both have the same state and rule in the same role in Kafka (the clean-shutdown marker; commit in memory at the in-sync set) and in VR Revisited (commit at a majority in memory). b's objection is that no system brings the replica back under a new identity. But that step is the published disk-incarnation rule with one more trigger. And the role, 'a replica that may lack what it acknowledged does not count again until it has caught up', is Kafka's (KIP-966 plus the in-sync rejoin) and VR's recovery. Its safety inside Raft was never modelled (K-09): a debt to DEV-03, not novelty. A close call.

mechanisms.name: None rung (a second delivery path)
mechanisms.option: none (P-06 asks for it in every row)
mechanisms.state: Not durable: messages published with durability none go straight to the current subscribers and never enter the log.
mechanisms.rules: Publish, then deliver in order per subject to every current subscriber, best effort. It has a failover rule of its own, which nobody has written (K-10).
mechanisms.source: REQUIREMENTS P-06; SPACE 2 Q `none`, SPACE 4.2 (every row counts it); AMENDMENTS 1.2 (not a fix; no experiment modelled its failover rule); E-02, E-08, E-09b (speed measured)
mechanisms.precedent: a: Redis sharded Pub/Sub (Redis 7.0, SPUBLISH and SSUBSCRIBE: a channel hashes to a slot; a message goes through that slot's shard to its current subscribers, at most once; a moved slot ends the subscription); NATS core publish and subscribe. | b: Core NATS publish and subscribe (at most once, in order, to the subscribers of the moment); Redis Pub/Sub, which in Redis Cluster is a second delivery path beside the replicated keyspace
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state (none that lasts), same rules (in order per subject, to the current subscribers, best effort), same role. SPACE's '1' counts a second path, not a new idea. Its failover rule is not written yet (K-10); when it is, it should be judged again. For V4 it applies only if v4 were built on. | b: No durable state. Same rules (straight to the current subscribers; nothing is logged; after a failover a subscriber subscribes again), same role. REQUIREMENTS X1 and SPACE 4.2 write 'counted in DEV-01', but DEV-01 lists only what has no precedent, and this is NATS core under another name. It is the same in all 20 rows, so no row moves against another. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Shared journal (group commit, cuts, segment indexes)
mechanisms.state: One journal per process holding every group's entries, terms and votes, chained and checksummed; cut records; then per-group segment files with indexes by offset, slot and partition; one reserve segment.
mechanisms.rules: One fdatasync covers a batch, and `persisted` waits for it. A follower writes a cut record before entries that replace its tail; the journal is truncated only once the segments that cover it are fsynced (A-09, A-25).
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 S `jrnl` (1 small: cuts, segment indexes); DESIGN-V5 4.1; AMENDMENTS A-09, A-25; E-12, E-29, E-35 (measured)
mechanisms.precedent: a: Apache BookKeeper's bookie storage (BookKeeper docs, 'Architecture': journals, entry logs, index files: every ledger's entries go to one journal with group commit; the ack waits for the journal's fsync; entries then go to entry logs with an index per ledger; the journal is trimmed only up to a checkpoint that the entry logs and indexes have synced). TiKV's raft-engine (one log for every region's entries and hard state). etcd's WAL for the chained checksum and for a later entry that replaces an earlier tail. EventStoreDB's index from stream to log position, for the index by partition. TiKV's storage.reserve-space, for the reserve. From memory. | b: Apache BookKeeper's bookie (one journal for every ledger, one fsync per batch, then indexed ledger storage; a journal file is removed only after a checkpoint has synced what it covers); TiKV's raft-engine (one log for every region, an index per region); CockroachDB's shared engine (a replaced Raft tail is deleted in the same batch as the new entries) and its emergency ballast file for the reserve
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state and rules in the same role. The explicit cut record and the index by slot are format choices on those designs (A-09 calls its six items format rules). SPACE's '1 small' is for exactly those two. | b: Same state (one journal per process for every group, then per-group files with indexes), same rules (group commit; a record that cuts a replaced tail; truncate only below what is synced elsewhere), same role. SPACE called it '1 small'. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: A write-ahead log per group
mechanisms.state: One log file per group (per partition in ISR, per resource in V4).
mechanisms.rules: Each group's appends are synced to its own file, so fsyncs grow with groups.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 S `walg`; etcd, Kafka; v4's WAL (CLAUDE.md); E-12 (measured: loses to a shared journal from 256 groups)
mechanisms.precedent: a: etcd's WAL; Kafka's log per partition. | b: etcd's WAL; Kafka's per-partition logs
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state, rule and role. | b: The published form. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: LSM store (log and state)
mechanisms.state: One LSM tree per member that holds the Raft log and the multi-version rows: memtables, sorted files and their compaction state.
mechanisms.rules: Writes go to a write-ahead log and a memtable, then to sorted files; compaction merges files and drops versions below the safe point.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 S `lsm`; TiKV on RocksDB; no experiment
mechanisms.precedent: a: RocksDB under TiKV; Pebble under CockroachDB. | b: TiKV on RocksDB; CockroachDB on Pebble
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: It is TiKV's own storage. PD only. | b: The published form. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Object-store tier (old segments and snapshot layers)
mechanisms.state: In the object store: uploaded old segments with their indexes, and snapshot layers with removal markers and merged bases, each named by an entry in the group's log.
mechanisms.rules: The leader uploads a segment or a snapshot (put-if-absent) and names it in the log only after the put is confirmed. A replica may drop its log below i only when a reachable snapshot covers i, the segment is uploaded or history allows it, and no slot move or fork still reads it.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 S `+tier` (1: snapshot layers against retention), SPACE 3 B0.O; DESIGN-V5 3.4 and 4.1 'The object store'; E-28 (measured)
mechanisms.precedent: a: For segments: Redpanda's Tiered Storage (the partition leader uploads a closed segment, then records it in the partition's own Raft log, and local data is deleted only up to what is uploaded; redpanda.com, 'tiered storage architecture deep dive', confirmed by search) and Kafka KIP-405. For snapshot layers against retention and forks: Neon (docs/pageserver-storage.md and the safekeeper: image and delta layers in the object store, merged by compaction; a safekeeper drops WAL only below both backup_lsn, the segment is uploaded, and remote_consistent_lsn, layers that cover it are uploaded; a branch keeps the layers it reads from being collected). Neon from memory. | b: Redpanda's tiered storage (the leader uploads a segment, then replicates an archival metadata command in the partition's own Raft log; local data is dropped only below what is uploaded); Kafka KIP-405; Neon (image and delta layers in the object store, merged in the background; the safekeepers drop WAL only below what the pageserver has made durable in the store; a branch pins its parent's history)
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state (old segments and snapshot layers in the object store, named in a log or manifest once the upload is confirmed), same rule (drop the local log only below what is uploaded and covered, and what no fork reads), same role (the home of history, of sleep and wake, and of forks). A close call: SPACE counts 1 for 'snapshot layers against retention', and DESIGN-V5 10.2 lists it among fero's own additions. | b: Same state (old segments and layered snapshots in an object store, named after the upload), same rules (upload, then name; drop the local log only below what is covered; a reader or a fork pins it), same role. SPACE counted 1 for 'snapshot layers against retention'; Neon has that coupling. Close call. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Restore mark in the store's manifest (an epoch high-water mark, and a session generation)
mechanisms.option: every row with a metadata group (A-08)
mechanisms.state: In the store's manifest (the home is open for rows that need no store): the highest epoch ever used (a slot's epoch; in a row with no slots, its unit's generation or the resource's incarnation); and a session generation that a restore raises.
mechanisms.rules: Every new epoch is recorded in the mark before it is used, so a slot move writes it. A restore takes an epoch above the mark and starts a new session generation; a retry from an older generation is refused, and a cursor the history does not hold is refused.
mechanisms.model: E-33: 8 rules by ablation (8 of 8 mutants); the store is always reachable in the model
mechanisms.source: AMENDMENTS A-08 (whether the mark is a mechanism is left to the counters; no precedent named) and section 4 (COMP's table); REQUIREMENTS OPS-07
mechanisms.precedent: None with the same rules. Nearest: PostgreSQL's timelines (timeline.c, findNewestTimeLine).
mechanisms.why: Novel, as both say: the nearest form is PostgreSQL's timelines (a restore takes a timeline above every history file in the archive), which neither records an epoch before use nor raises a session generation; E-33 names no precedent. Rows: a is right on PD. In PD's row, positions and lock tokens are the oracle's timestamps; the oracle saves its high-water before use, outside the data a restore brings back (timestamp-oracle, not novel by both), and D `txn` has no sessions to cut. AMENDMENTS A-08 lists PD as unchanged. The other 17 rows keep it. One unit, not two: both counters keep the count at 1; its two pieces of state are written by one protocol, E-33's 8 rules.

mechanisms.name: Fold on every full replica
mechanisms.state: On each full replica: the rows of the partitions its groups hold, folded by `data` from committed records in log order.
mechanisms.rules: Apply each committed record once, in offset order, through data's hot lane; never re-run a condition or an op. A new leader folds its whole log before it answers; a moved slot's rows are taken from exactly one group.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 F `all`, SPACE 1 B0; DESIGN-V5 4.3 'The fold'; E-05, E-34, E-43 (measured)
mechanisms.precedent: a: State machine replication as Raft has it (ATC 2014, section 5.3: every server applies committed entries in log order); etcd's apply loop. | b: Raft paper section 5.3 (each server applies committed entries in log order); etcd's apply loop
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state, rules and role. 'A moved slot's rows come from exactly one group' is a slot-move rule. | b: Same state, same rules, same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Fold on the leader only, with one warm standby
mechanisms.state: On the leader and on one warm standby: the rows of the group's partitions; the other followers keep the log only.
mechanisms.rules: Only the leader and the standby apply committed records. A failover to the standby is warm; to any other replica it is a cold rebuild from a snapshot and the tail, so the standby is required (A-26).
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 F `ldr`, SPACE 3 R1.LF; AMENDMENTS A-26 (E-05 measured; reasoned for SIDE and OBJ)
mechanisms.precedent: a: Kafka Streams with num.standby.replicas=1 (the active task folds; one standby keeps a warm copy from the changelog; any other instance rebuilds cold). | b: Kafka Streams with one standby replica (num.standby.replicas = 1: the active task folds, one standby keeps a warm copy, any other instance rebuilds from the changelog)
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state, rules and role. | b: Same state, same rules, same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Lazy fold on followers
mechanisms.state: On a follower: rows folded behind the log, or on first read.
mechanisms.rules: A follower folds when it is asked or idle, and serves a read only once its fold has reached the position asked for.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 F `lazy` (1 novel); Kafka Streams standbys; no experiment
mechanisms.precedent: a: Neon's pageserver (it applies WAL when a page is asked for, and a read at a position waits until the WAL up to it has arrived); TiKV's follower read (wait until the apply index reaches the read index). From memory. | b: Tango (Balakrishnan et al., SOSP 2013: an object's view is played forward from the shared log when it is read); TiKV's follower read waits until its applied index reaches the read index
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state, rules and role. OBJ only. | b: Same state, same rules (fold when asked; serve only once the fold has reached the position), same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Fold-version entry
mechanisms.state: A committed entry in each group's log that names the fold version in force from that offset (data's build and fero's L2 library).
mechanisms.rules: A replica never folds an entry under another version than the one in force at its offset, and refuses to serve until it runs that version. A roll raises the version only after every replica has said it can run it.
mechanisms.source: REQUIREMENTS OPS-12; AMENDMENTS A-10 (five pins for the fold version) and section 4 (COMP's table); precedent on offer: CockroachDB's cluster versions; E-43 (measured); for V4 it would apply only if v4 were built on
mechanisms.precedent: a: etcd's cluster version (set by a request through the Raft log once every member can run it); CockroachDB's cluster version with the per-range Migrate command; Kafka's metadata.version, a FeatureLevelRecord in the KRaft log (KIP-778). | b: Kafka KIP-584 and metadata.version (a finalized feature level is a record in the metadata log, raised only when every broker supports it); etcd's cluster version, set through Raft as the lowest member version; CockroachDB's cluster version; Cosmos SDK x/upgrade (a plan in the log takes effect at a height and an old binary stops there)
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state (an entry in the log that names the version in force from there), same rules (replicas act by the version in force at that point; it rises only when every replica can run it), same role. For V4 it applies only if v4 were built on. | b: Same state (a log entry that names the version in force from that point), same rules, same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Subscribe (cursors, snapshot then deltas, END and expired)
mechanisms.option: any (and every row that serves subscriptions, A-06)
mechanisms.state: Held by the subscriber: a cursor of the cluster id, the resource's incarnation and, per slot, its epoch and the last sequence seen (a durable row only for a consumer). On the server, not durable: the index of partitions to subscribers. AMENDMENTS section 4 lists this piece as no mechanism by DEV-10 (a)'s letter.
mechanisms.rules: A ready replica serves up to the commit offset, and never before its fold has reached the cursor. A replica that lacks the reader's next record answers END, and only the leader of the group that holds the slot says expired (A-06). A snapshot replaces; a cursor of an older epoch is refused unknown-log.
mechanisms.model: E-31: 26 rules by ablation, 27 with the move's carried segment names (31 of 32 mutants)
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 W `any`; DESIGN-V5 4.4; AMENDMENTS A-06 (a changed answer) and section 4 (COMP's table); PD has no `any` but must serve subscriptions (P-03, P-05, P-07)
mechanisms.precedent: a: Couchbase DCP (kv_engine, docs/dcp: a stream request carries the vBucket UUID and seqno; a snapshot marker, then mutations; 'stream end' when the vBucket moves; a rollback when the cursor is ahead). Kafka KIP-392 (a follower serves only up to its high watermark; a follower that lacks the offset sends the client to the leader, which alone decides 'out of range') and KIP-320 (a cursor's epoch is checked). Kubernetes list-then-watch with '410 Gone', for a snapshot that replaces. | b: Couchbase DCP stream requests (a cursor of vBucket UUID and seqno; a snapshot marker, then mutations; a stream end when the vBucket moved; a rollback answer); Kafka's fetch from a follower (KIP-392) with leader epoch checks (KIP-320) and committed offsets for a consumer; etcd's watch from a revision, with ErrCompacted
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same rules in the same role. A-06's fix is KIP-392's rule. Conflation per row for a slow reader and read credits are published too (Solace's message eliding; AMQP link credit). The cursor is held by the subscriber and the index is in memory, so by DEV-10 (a)'s letter it is not a mechanism; AMENDMENTS section 4 says the same. | b: Mostly no durable state (AMENDMENTS section 4 lists it as no mechanism). Same rules (serve up to the commit point; snapshot, then deltas; 'go elsewhere' against 'expired'; an old epoch is refused), same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Lease reads
mechanisms.state: Not durable: the leader's read lease, a time promise that no other leader exists until it ends.
mechanisms.rules: A leader that holds an unexpired lease answers a read from its own state, with no round to the majority. It needs bounded clock drift.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 W `lease`; CockroachDB, Spanner, TiKV's leader lease; no experiment (G-25)
mechanisms.precedent: a: Ongaro's thesis, section 6.4.1 (leases); TiKV's leader lease; CockroachDB's leaseholder. | b: Ongaro's thesis section 6.4.1 (lease reads); CockroachDB's leases; etcd's raft ReadOnlyLeaseBased
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same rule in the same role. Not durable. | b: The published form. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Forwarding (any server takes a write and forwards it to the leader)
mechanisms.option: fwd (the base in every row: browsers need it)
mechanisms.state: Not durable: a server's route view (from the #meta copy every member follows) and the writes it holds in flight for a leader.
mechanisms.rules: A server forwards a write only over the link to the leader it had when it took the write, and each copy only once. A stale route costs one moved; a member that cannot forward refuses at once with a redirect, and never drops or holds the write (A-02, A-21).
mechanisms.model: E-20: the hop rule `forward.once` is counted inside each dedup option (1 rule under `sess`, 2 under `win`)
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 Y `fwd`; DESIGN-V5 4.2 'Routing' and 4.3 'No late arrivals'; AMENDMENTS A-02, A-21 and section 2 Y; E-01 (hop cost measured)
mechanisms.precedent: a: etcd's raft (a follower forwards a proposal to its leader once, and drops it when it knows none); CockroachDB's NotLeaseHolderError redirect; Redis Cluster's MOVED. | b: ZooKeeper followers forward a write to the leader, one hop; etcd's raft forwards a proposal to the leader and answers ErrProposalDropped when it has none; Raft paper section 8 (a follower redirects the client); Redis Cluster's MOVED
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same rules in the same role. Not durable. | b: No durable state. Same rules (forward once to the known leader; else refuse at once with a redirect), same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Smart clients (the client caches slot to leader)
mechanisms.state: In each client: a cached table of slot (or range, or partition) to leader, at most one entry per slot of a resource.
mechanisms.rules: The client sends a write straight to the cached leader and follows MOVED or ASK during a move, refreshing its table.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 Y `smart`; Redis Cluster, Kafka clients, the TiKV client; its MOVED and ASK path was never examined (G-25)
mechanisms.precedent: a: Redis Cluster clients (MOVED and ASK); Kafka clients' metadata cache; TiKV's client region cache. | b: Redis Cluster clients (a slot table in the client; MOVED and ASK); Kafka clients' metadata cache
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state, rules and role. | b: The published form. BUY's smart client is the bought system's own, so BUY is left out as the list has it. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Group-to-worker map (N kernel workers)
mechanisms.state: Per process: which kernel worker each group is pinned to, with one journal per worker.
mechanisms.rules: The main thread routes each message to its group's worker; a group stays on its worker; messages between workers are recorded as inputs.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 M `kwN` (0-1: a group-to-worker map) and SPACE 5 (kwN: a journal per worker); TiKV's raftstore pool; not measured in a native build (G-25)
mechanisms.precedent: a: Redpanda's shard_table (each Raft group is pinned to one core; cores pass messages with Seastar's submit_to); ScyllaDB's commit log per shard; TiKV's raftstore pool. From memory. | b: Redpanda's shard table (each Raft group is pinned to one core; other cores hand work over with Seastar's submit_to); CockroachDB's Raft scheduler shards
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state, rules and role. | b: Same state, same rules, same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Local seam between the daemon and the app (a shared-memory ring)
mechanisms.state: Not durable: a shared-memory ring between the host's daemon and the app's Node process, holding batches on their way to the app's L2 and fold, and results on their way back.
mechanisms.rules: The daemon holds L0, L1 and fan-out. It hands the app the batches of the groups this host leads and appends only what the app returns (A-30: a ring, not a socket).
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 H `side` (novel 1: the local seam); AMENDMENTS A-30; E-03 (measured)
mechanisms.precedent: a: Not a mechanism by DEV-10 (a)'s letter: it names no durable or replicated state. Its nearest published forms: Aeron Cluster (the consensus module and the clustered service are joined by Aeron IPC, a shared-memory ring, so a stalled service does not stop replication), and Dapr's sidecar, which calls the app for the actors placed on its host. From memory. | b: Aeron Cluster (the consensus module and the clustered service are separate agents, or processes, joined by Aeron IPC: shared-memory log buffers); Dapr and Envoy sidecars for the role split
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: The ring is a transport that carries the kernel's five operations to a local process. A shared-memory ring between a daemon and its client is published (Aeron's media driver), and so is a consensus daemon kept apart from the app's code. The rule 'append only what the app returns' is K `lib`'s seam moved across a process line. SPACE counts 1, and I am not sure one system has the very same rules, so this is a close call. SIDE only. | b: It holds no durable or replicated state, so by DEV-10 (a)'s letter it is no mechanism. As a seam it is published: a replication daemon and the app's state machine joined by a shared-memory ring. SPACE counted 1. Close call; it touches SIDE only. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Calls routed to the partition's leader
mechanisms.state: Not durable: calls in flight at a partition leader's host.
mechanisms.rules: A call goes to its partition's leader and runs there; a call in flight across a handover is refused or re-run at the new leader.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 U `ldr` (1: in-flight calls across a handover); AMENDMENTS section 2 U (E-22: it buys no safety)
mechanisms.precedent: a: Orleans (Bykov et al., 'Orleans: Distributed Virtual Actors', MSR-TR-2014-41: a call goes to the grain's one activation; a call cut off by a failure fails and is retried); Cloudflare Durable Objects; Redis Functions, which run at the master. | b: Cloudflare Durable Objects; Orleans grains; VoltDB procedures run at the partition's leader
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same rule in the same role. Not durable. SIDE only. | b: No durable state. Same rule (a call runs at the unit's one owner; a call in flight across a handover fails or runs again), same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Admission credits (a credit window on the client wire)
mechanisms.state: No durable or replicated state is named (A-07 leaves open whether this is a mechanism): how many writes each client or link may have outstanding, and a budget of TLS handshakes per tick at the edge.
mechanisms.rules: A client holds at most its granted number of writes outstanding; the rest wait in the client and fail at their deadline. The server hands out the grant; that part was not built.
mechanisms.source: AMENDMENTS A-07 (E-39 measured with a fixed client-side window; no precedent named; AMQP link credit and HTTP/2 windows cited from memory); REQUIREMENTS F-19; for V4 it would apply only if v4 were built on
mechanisms.precedent: a: Breakwater (Cho et al., OSDI 2020, sections 4 and 5: the server hands out credits from its own queueing delay; a client sends only with a credit and holds the rest; confirmed by search). HTTP/2's SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS (RFC 9113, section 5.1.2). AMQP 1.0 link credit (section 2.6.7). For the handshake budget: HAProxy's maxsslrate. | b: HTTP/2 SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS (RFC 9113 section 5.1.2) and QUIC MAX_STREAMS (RFC 9000 section 4.6): the server grants how many requests a client may have open; AMQP 1.0 link credit; RSocket's LEASE frame; HAProxy maxsslrate for a budget of TLS handshakes per second
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state (how many requests a client may have outstanding, granted by the server), same rules, same role (overload). E-39 named no precedent; these are it. By DEV-10 (a)'s letter it has no durable state. The grant from the server was not built here. For V4 it applies only if v4 were built on. | b: REQUIREMENTS X17 says to count admission control and to prefer a published fix. Same state (a grant per client link), same rules (the client never holds more than the grant outstanding; the rest wait in the client), same role (keep goodput under overload). The server-side grant was not built here; a row can take the published form as it is. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Tenant byte budget on a shared tier or pool
mechanisms.state: No durable or replicated state is named (A-29 leaves open whether this is a mechanism): a byte budget per tenant per second in a process that pools tenants.
mechanisms.rules: The tier or pool holds a tenant's bytes back past its budget (about 1 MiB/s of big-record bytes on this disk), so one tenant at its quota does not raise another's p99. A volume per tenant needs no such rule.
mechanisms.source: AMENDMENTS A-29 (E-35 measured the ratios; the budget was not built; no precedent named); REQUIREMENTS OPS-14, SC-11
mechanisms.precedent: a: Kafka's quotas (KIP-13: a byte-rate quota per client or user on a shared broker; the broker holds back a client that passes it); Pulsar's publish-rate limits per namespace; CockroachDB's per-tenant admission control. | b: Kafka's quotas (KIP-13: a byte rate per client, held back by the broker); CockroachDB's tenant rate limiter (pkg/kv/kvserver/tenantrate: a token bucket of bytes per tenant)
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state (a byte budget per tenant), same rule (hold back the tenant past it), same role (neighbours on one disk). E-35 named no precedent; this is it. By DEV-10 (a)'s letter it has no durable state. Not built here. | b: No durable state. Same state (a byte budget per tenant in a shared process), same rule, same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Disk incarnation and checksum (a damaged replica rejoins as new)
mechanisms.state: Per dir: a random 128-bit incarnation written when the dir is made; per record a checksum and its predecessor's offset.
mechanisms.rules: A checksum per entry turns damage into a wipe, and a wiped or new disk takes a new incarnation that never votes as the replica it replaced (A-28). Only a tail that the checksum shows was never acknowledged is cut. The same rule brings back as new a replica that stopped uncleanly under `memory`, and one whose store a failed fsync condemned (DESIGN-V5 4.1: one rule, three triggers).
mechanisms.model: E-37 (TLC on etcd's spec, three voters): 2 rules, both needed
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 Z `rejoin` (1 small); DESIGN-V5 4.1; AMENDMENTS A-28 (reasoned for SLOG)
mechanisms.precedent: a: Chandra, Griesemer and Redstone, 'Paxos Made Live' (PODC 2007), section 5.1, 'Handling disk corruption': checksums find the damage, a marker tells a wiped disk from a new replica, and the replica rebuilds as a non-voting member (confirmed by search). Alagappan et al., 'Protocol-Aware Recovery' (FAST 2018) lists the same answer among the known ones. Kafka KIP-858's directory id. etcd's chained WAL checksum and its repair of a torn tail. | b: Kafka KIP-853 (a directory id made when the log dir is formatted; a voter is (node id, directory id), so a replaced disk is not the old voter and joins by AddVoter); CockroachDB's StoreIdent (a wiped disk gets a new store id); etcd's WAL (a chained CRC; only a torn tail is repaired, other damage means the member is replaced); Chandra et al., 'Paxos Made Live', PODC 2007, section 5.1 (checksums; a replica that lost its disk state does not vote at first)
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state (an id per disk; a checksum per record), same rules (damage or a new disk means: come back with no vote under the old identity; only an unacknowledged torn tail is cut), same role. E-37 confirmed the 2 rules on etcd's spec. | b: Same state (an incarnation per dir, a checksum per record), same rules (damage means a wipe; a wiped disk is a new replica that never votes as the old one; only a torn, never acknowledged tail is cut), same role. SPACE called it '1 small'. KIP-853 checked on the web on 2026-11-10; the rest cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism. State names changed by a regrouping the referee took (see disagreements).

mechanisms.name: Founding by a conditional create of the cluster id
mechanisms.option: A-08: rows that require an object store across boxes
mechanisms.state: The cluster id, created once in the object store (If-None-Match), then held in every dir's boot record and in #meta's first entry.
mechanisms.rules: The create succeeds only while no id is stored; the seed whose create succeeds is #meta's only voter; every other seed adopts only the stored id and is added by healing. `seeds` never runs beside a dir that holds an id. On one box the same rule uses an exclusive create of the cluster-id file.
mechanisms.model: E-33: 4 rules by ablation (4 of 4 mutants); one box 4 rules, 5 with the exclusive create (reasoned)
mechanisms.source: AMENDMENTS A-08 (E-33 calls it 'new here'; S3 conditional writes are the cited base); SPACE 4.1 footnote 1; DESIGN-V5 4.2 'Clusters, genesis and discovery'
mechanisms.precedent: a: Patroni's 'initialize' key (Patroni docs, patroni.dcs: initialize() must create the key atomically; the node that wins bootstraps alone and the cluster's system identifier is stored there; every other node joins as a replica only once the key exists; a node whose data carries another identifier is refused; confirmed by search). S3's If-None-Match is the same create-if-absent on an object store. Also Kafka's /cluster/id (KIP-78). | b: Patroni's /initialize key (patroni/ha.py bootstrap): the first node to create the key in the DCS, an atomic create-if-absent, founds the cluster alone and writes its system id there; every other node joins it as a replica; a data dir with another id is refused ('system ID mismatch'). S3's If-None-Match is the same create-if-absent on an object store
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state (one id, made once in an outside store by create-if-absent, then kept in every dir), same rules (the winner founds alone; the others adopt the stored id and join), same role (exactly one cluster from racing starters). E-33 calls it 'new here'; it is Patroni's bootstrap with an object store in place of etcd. | b: Same state (the cluster's id, created once in an outside store and kept in every dir), same rules (only the winner of the create founds; the others adopt the stored id; a dir with an id never founds again), same role. E-33 calls it 'new here'; it is Patroni's race under another store. checked on the web on 2026-11-10.

mechanisms.name: Founding by one fero init
mechanisms.option: A-08: rows that require no object store across boxes
mechanisms.state: The cluster id, minted by one operator step, then held in every dir's boot record and in #meta's first entry.
mechanisms.rules: Init runs once and mints the id; a seed never founds by itself and adopts only an id it finds at a seed it reaches. `seeds` never runs beside a dir that holds an id. On one box an exclusive create of the cluster-id file founds.
mechanisms.model: E-33: 3 rules by ablation (3 of 3 mutants); one box 4 rules, 5 with the exclusive create (reasoned)
mechanisms.source: AMENDMENTS A-08; CockroachDB's init; PD's initial cluster and KRaft's storage format for PD and ISR
mechanisms.precedent: a: CockroachDB's 'cockroach init'; KRaft's 'kafka-storage format --cluster-id'; PD's initial-cluster. | b: CockroachDB's `cockroach init` (run once; the cluster id is kept in every store); Kafka KRaft's `kafka-storage format --cluster-id`
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state, rules and role. E-33 says the same. | b: Same state, same rules, same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Writer epoch on log members (rlog)
mechanisms.state: In the log group's log: writer entries, each naming the server that is the group's writer and its epoch; every append carries the writer's epoch.
mechanisms.rules: The controller hands the role over only when the writer is gone to it and only to a linked server, by committing a writer entry with the next epoch. The new writer folds to the log's end before it writes, and the log group's leader takes an append only with the latest committed writer epoch (A-14).
mechanisms.model: E-16: 9 rules by ablation, all needed (9 of 9 non-equivalent mutants)
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 R `rlog` (about 1: the writer-epoch check), SPACE 3 RL1; AMENDMENTS A-14; Kafka producer epochs, BookKeeper fencing, Neon's safekeepers
mechanisms.precedent: Amazon MemoryDB (Taleb et al., SIGMOD 2024, DOI 10.1145/3626246.3653380, section 4): the primary is a server outside the transaction log; it takes leadership by appending a leadership entry with a conditional append that names the entry it follows, so only a replica caught up to the log's end can win, and the old primary's appends then fail; leases are renewed by log entries. Checked here through reviews of the paper found by web search (the paper itself and two blogs were not reachable from this session). Kafka's producer epochs (KIP-98): a coordinator bumps the epoch in a committed record, every batch carries it, and the partition leader refuses an older one.
mechanisms.why: Referee. b's reason was that in every precedent it knew, the writer is the log's own proposer or the epoch lives in a metadata store. MemoryDB is the case b missed: a writer outside the log, a leadership entry inside the log, appends tied to it, and the new writer caught up first. That RLOG's controller commits the entry, rather than the writer itself, is the controller's part (controller-commands, counted there), and a coordinator that bumps an epoch is Kafka's. SPACE estimated about 1; A-14's 9 rules stay as rules (E-16). A close call. RLOG only.

mechanisms.name: Loglets on log nodes
mechanisms.state: Per loglet: its entries on a set of log nodes, and the last entry a write quorum of them holds.
mechanisms.rules: The group's writer appends each batch to the loglet's log nodes; a batch is committed when a write quorum holds it on disk.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 R `slog`, SPACE 3 SL1; V5-REPLICATION, V5-LOG-FIRST-REVIEW; Delos, BookKeeper; not modelled here
mechanisms.precedent: a: Apache BookKeeper ledgers (ensemble, write quorum, ack quorum); Delos loglets (Balakrishnan et al., OSDI 2020). | b: Apache BookKeeper ledgers (an ensemble, a write quorum, an ack quorum); Delos loglets (Balakrishnan et al., OSDI 2020)
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state, rules and role. SLOG only. | b: Same state, same rules, same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Seal and recovery
mechanisms.state: Per loglet and log node: a sealed flag; and the recovered end of a sealed loglet.
mechanisms.rules: A sealed log node takes no more appends to that loglet. A new writer seals enough nodes to block a write quorum, reads forward to find the end, and writes the tail again to a quorum before the chain is closed.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 R `slog` (seal + metadata CAS); V5-LOG-FIRST-REVIEW F1, F2, F4; not modelled here
mechanisms.precedent: a: BookKeeper's fencing and ledger recovery (the new writer fences enough bookies, reads forward, writes the tail again, then closes the ledger); Delos's seal (OSDI 2020, section 3). The rule 'unknown is not absent' (V5-LOG-FIRST-REVIEW F1) is the one Vanlightly's TLA+ work found for BookKeeper. | b: BookKeeper's ledger recovery (fence the bookies, read forward, write the tail again, close the ledger); Delos's seal and checkTail; Corfu's seal
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state, rules and role. SLOG only. | b: Same state, same rules, same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Loglet chain (metadata compare-and-swap)
mechanisms.state: In the metadata group, per data group: the chain of its loglets, each with its log nodes, its start and, once closed, its end.
mechanisms.rules: The chain changes only by compare-and-swap: one step closes the open loglet at its recovered end and opens the next on a chosen set of log nodes.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 R `slog`, SPACE 5 (slog: C needs a CAS register); V5-LOG-FIRST-REVIEW F3, F5; not modelled here
mechanisms.precedent: a: Delos's VirtualLog: a chain of loglets in the MetaStore, changed by compare-and-swap (OSDI 2020, section 3); Pulsar's managed ledger, a list of ledgers in the metadata store. | b: Delos's VirtualLog MetaStore (a chain of loglets changed by a versioned conditional write); Pulsar's managed ledger list in its metadata store
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state, rule and role. SLOG only. | b: Same state, same rules, same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Writer assignment on a shared log (slog)
mechanisms.state: In the metadata group, per data group: the server that is its writer, and the epoch of that role.
mechanisms.rules: The controller names a new writer when the old one's session lapses; the new writer seals the open loglet, which fences the old writer. The writer changes its own log nodes; the controller changes writers.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 4.1 footnote 5 and V5-LOG-FIRST-REVIEW F3; not modelled here
mechanisms.precedent: a: Apache Pulsar: a broker takes a topic through the metadata store, and opening the topic's ledger with recovery fences the old owner; the writer changes its own ensemble (BookKeeper), the load manager changes owners. From memory. | b: Apache Pulsar: a topic's owner broker is named in the metadata store; a new owner opens the managed ledger, which fences the old owner's ledger; the owner itself changes its bookies
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state, rules and role. V5-LOG-FIRST-REVIEW counts 'controller against writer' as novel in the log-first draft; with F3's rule (the writer changes its nodes, the controller changes writers) it is Pulsar's split. SLOG only. | b: Same state, same rules (the controller names the writer; the seal fences the old one; the writer changes its own log nodes), same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Sessions to the controller (the failure detector)
mechanisms.option: failure detector: sessions to the controller
mechanisms.state: Per member: a session with the controller, kept by heartbeats, with an epoch that rises each time the member registers.
mechanisms.rules: A member whose heartbeats stop for the session timeout is fenced; it must register again, with a new epoch, before it leads, writes or joins an in-sync set.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 C (the failure detector sub-choice: sessions to the controller); Kafka's broker heartbeats to its controller, TiKV's store heartbeats to PD; E-25 (SLOG: 400 idle frames a second)
mechanisms.precedent: a: Kafka's broker heartbeats and broker epoch (KIP-631); ZooKeeper sessions; TiKV's store heartbeats to PD. | b: Kafka KRaft broker heartbeats and broker epochs (KIP-631: a broker whose heartbeats stop is fenced and must register again); TiKV's store heartbeats to PD
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: Same state, rules and role. | b: Same state, same rules, same role. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Partition log (the leader appends, followers fetch)
mechanisms.state: Each replica's log of one partition: records with their offsets and the leader epoch they were written in.
mechanisms.rules: Only the partition's leader appends; followers fetch from it and append in order.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 R `isr`, SPACE 3 I1; Kafka; not modelled here
mechanisms.precedent: a: Kafka's partition log with leader epochs (KIP-101). | b: Kafka's partition log and follower fetch
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: It is Kafka's own mechanism. ISR only. | b: The published mechanism. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: In-sync set
mechanisms.state: Per partition, in the controller's log: the in-sync replica set.
mechanisms.rules: The leader asks the controller to drop a follower that falls behind and to add one that has caught up to the high watermark; only a registered, unfenced replica may join.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 R `isr` (Kafka ISR + KRaft: KIP-841, KIP-903), SPACE 5 (isr forces cent); not modelled here
mechanisms.precedent: a: Kafka's in-sync replica set under KRaft (KIP-841, KIP-903). | b: Kafka's in-sync replicas under KRaft (AlterPartition; KIP-841, KIP-903)
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: It is Kafka's own mechanism. ISR only. | b: The published mechanism. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: High watermark
mechanisms.state: Per partition: the offset up to which every member of the in-sync set holds the log.
mechanisms.rules: The leader advances it to the lowest log end of the in-sync set. A write with acks=all is answered when the high watermark passes it; readers see only records below it.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 Q `isr`, R `isr`; Kafka acks=all with min.insync.replicas; not modelled here
mechanisms.precedent: a: Kafka's high watermark with acks=all and min.insync.replicas. | b: Kafka's high watermark with acks=all and min.insync.replicas
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: It is Kafka's own mechanism. ISR only. | b: The published mechanism. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Leader epoch
mechanisms.state: Per partition: the leader and its epoch, set by the controller; each replica keeps the start offset of every epoch.
mechanisms.rules: The controller picks a new leader from the in-sync set (or the eligible leaders) and bumps the epoch. A follower truncates its log to the end of the last epoch it shares with the leader before it fetches.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 R `isr` (KIP-101, KIP-279, KIP-320); not modelled here
mechanisms.precedent: a: Kafka's leader epoch (KIP-101, KIP-279, KIP-320). | b: Kafka's leader epoch (KIP-101, KIP-279, KIP-320)
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: It is Kafka's own mechanism. ISR only. | b: The published mechanism. cited from memory, sure of the system and the mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Eligible leader replicas
mechanisms.state: Per partition, in the controller's log: replicas that left the in-sync set while holding everything up to the high watermark.
mechanisms.rules: When the in-sync set falls below the minimum, the controller keeps the leavers as eligible leaders, and elects only from the in-sync set or from them.
mechanisms.source: SPACE 2 R `isr` (KIP-966); not modelled here
mechanisms.precedent: a: Kafka's eligible leader replicas (KIP-966). | b: Kafka KIP-966 (eligible leader replicas)
mechanisms.why: Both counters agree. a: A published description (the KIP), in Kafka since 3.7. ISR only. | b: The published mechanism. checked on the web on 2026-11-10.

mechanisms.name: Log objects (a commit is a PUT)
mechanisms.state: Per group: its log as numbered objects in the object store.
